conversation.content:
Good morning—thank you for coming in today. My name is Maya Bennett, and I’m a perinatal mental-health clinician here at the clinic. I specialize in helping new mothers adjust emotionally after birth, and I’m really glad you’re here.

I’d like to spend the next few minutes doing a short screening called the **Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale**—often shortened to the **EPDS**. It’s a simple, 10-question check-in that looks at how you’ve been feeling emotionally and mentally over the past week. It’s not a test of your parenting or a judgment of how you “should” feel; it’s just a tool to help us understand how best to support you.

Everything we discuss stays confidential between you and our care team; the only exception would be if I felt you might be in immediate danger, and then we’d work together on next steps. We’ll go through each question one by one. Some will feel easy, others a little harder—take your time, and answer in whatever way feels most true for you.

Ready to begin?  
Here’s the first question:

Over the past seven days, have you still been able to enjoy the little things that used to make you happy—like a favorite song, a warm drink, or a quick hello from a friend—or has that joy felt out of reach?

Honestly, not really. I used to love my morning coffee and putting on a podcast while I folded laundry, but lately it all just feels… flat. I’ll catch myself halfway through the cup and realize I didn’t even taste it. Same when my neighbor waved at me yesterday—I waved back, but it didn’t give me that little lift it used to.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things

Sometimes I’ll hear a joke or see something silly the baby does and a little laugh slips out, but it feels forced—like I have to remind myself “this is supposed to be funny.” Most of the time I’m just too tired or down to find things genuinely amusing.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

Not much. When my sister mentioned grabbing coffee next week, I said “sure,” but inside I felt… nothing. Even little outings feel like chores. I used to get excited about small plans—now it’s like I’m just ticking boxes so people stop worrying.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

All the time. Yesterday the baby spit up a ton after feeding and I immediately thought, “I must’ve over-fed him or held him wrong.” When he wouldn’t settle at 3 a.m., I kept replaying everything I’d done—maybe I ate something that upset my milk, maybe I didn’t burp him long enough. My partner says it’s normal baby stuff, but I can’t shake the feeling that I’m just not getting it right.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Yeah, pretty much every day. I’ll be folding onesies and suddenly my chest feels tight—like something awful is about to happen, even though nothing’s wrong. I’ll check the baby monitor twenty times, convinced he’s stopped breathing, or worry the bath water was too hot and he’ll get sick later. I know it sounds crazy, but I can’t turn the “what-ifs” off.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

Yes, a few times this week. Once, I was just walking to the kitchen and my heart started racing, I felt shaky, like I couldn’t get enough air. I had to sit down and grip the counter because I thought I might pass out. Nothing triggered it—no loud noise, no bad thoughts—just this sudden wave of panic that came out of nowhere and left me rattled for the rest of the evening.
Things have been getting on top of me

Yeah, most days it feels like I’m drowning in small stuff. Dishes pile up, the baby needs feeding, laundry’s everywhere, and I just stand there paralyzed, thinking, “I can’t do all this.” I usually push through, but it’s like I’m barely treading water—always on edge that one extra thing will make me snap.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

Yes. I’ll lie down exhausted, but my head won’t quit replaying every little thing I might have messed up—did I fasten the swaddle tight enough, did I sanitize the bottles right, am I already failing him at two weeks? Some nights I watch the clock slide past 2 a.m., 3 a.m., and I still can’t settle, even when the baby’s quiet. It’s like the sadness keeps me wired.
I have felt sad or miserable

Pretty much every day this week. It’s like a heavy blanket I can’t shake off—nothing feels bright, and I catch myself tearing up over tiny things, like a lullaby or the way his tiny socks look in the dryer. I keep thinking I should be glowing, but mostly I just feel hollow and weepy.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

Yeah… I’ve cried three times since last Monday. The worst was two nights ago—he wouldn’t latch, I felt like my milk was failing him, and I just sat in the glider with tears running down while he fussed. I kept telling myself to get it together, but the tears kept coming.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
No, nothing like that. I feel overwhelmed and sad, but I’ve never thought about hurting myself. I just want to feel better so I can be the mom he deserves.

I hear how heavy these early weeks have felt for you-how even the small rituals that once brought comfort, like savoring your morning coffee or sharing a laugh, now seem distant and colorless. You described a daily weight of <sym>sadness</sym> and <sym>worry</sym> that follows you from daylight tasks to the quiet of night, alongside sudden waves of <sym>panic</sym> that rise without warning. Yet through it all you remain devoted to your baby, yearning simply to feel well enough to be the mother you want to be.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 24, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>definitely not so much now</sym>, <sym>Patient reports anhedonia with clear loss of anticipatory pleasure, describing emotional numbness and obligatory participation, aligning with "Hardly at all."</sym>, <sym>Response shows pervasive self-blame occurring "All the time," directly matching the highest severity option.</sym>, <sym>Patient reports daily, intrusive, unprovoked anxiety with somatic symptoms and repetitive catastrophic worries, matching 'Yes, very often</sym>, <sym>The response describes multiple discrete episodes of unexpected panic with physical symptoms, matching "Yes, sometimes" rather than frequent or constant panic.</sym>, <sym>Patient describes daily overwhelm, paralysis, and fear of snapping, aligning with "most of the time I haven't been able to cope at all."</sym>, <sym>Patient describes nightly insomnia driven by intrusive anxious thoughts, watching hours pass without being able to settle, matching 'Yes, most of the time</sym>, <sym>"Yes, most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports multiple crying episodes in the past week tied to distress about breastfeeding, matching "Yes, quite often"</sym>)
**Reasoning:** An EPDS total ≥14 signals high likelihood of major depressive episode; at 24, well above threshold, symptoms align with <med>DSM-5 criteria for Major Depressive Disorder with Peripartum Onset</med>: depressed mood most of the day, markedly diminished interest or pleasure, self-reproach, anxiety, and sleep disturbance causing clinically significant distress. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange urgent same-week appointment with <med>obstetric or primary care provider</med> for full evaluation
2. Request formal referral to <med>perinatal mental-health specialist</med> for therapy and medication consult if indicated
3. Encourage 15-20 minutes of daylight or gentle stroller walk daily to support circadian rhythm and mild exercise
4. Practice 4-7-8 breathing when <sym>panic sensations</sym> emerge; pair with grounding technique (name 5 things you see, 4 you feel, 3 you hear)
5. Share <med>Postpartum Support International</med> warm-line 1-800-944-4773 and local mom-and-baby support group contacts
6. Schedule daily check-in with partner or trusted adult to review mood, infant care tasks, and respite needs
7. Plan re-screen in two weeks to monitor symptom trajectory and intervention response
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

stats.query:
postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 24: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening – 2 wks post-delivery

Areas endorsed (EPDS scoring guide):
- Items 1, 2 (laugh/look-forward): 1 pt each – marked anhedonia, loss of enjoyment
- Items 3, 4, 5 (guilt, worry, panic): 3 pts each – excessive self-blame, intrusive “what-ifs,” sudden physiologic panic episodes
- Item 6 (coping): 3 pts – daily sense of “drowning,” task paralysis
- Items 7, 8, 9 (sleep, mood, crying): 3 pts each – mood-congruent insomnia, pervasive sadness, tearfulness
- Item 10 (self-harm): 0 pt – denies; no safety concern at present

Pattern: High endorsement of affective/anxiety items; low endorsement of anhedonia items; no self-harm ideation.

Clinical significance:
- Meets screening threshold for likely major depressive episode with anxious features (EPDS total ≥ 12 plus prominent anxiety items)
- Postpartum onset ≤ 4 wks
- Functional impact: disrupted sleep, impaired bonding confidence, avoidance of outings
- Protective factor: support person present; no self-harm thoughts

Recommendation: Refer for expedited perinatal-behavioral-health evaluation; consider PHQ-9/GAD-7; monitor safety at every contact.
